# The exact three-parameter image of strict triangle row data

This note describes the ordinary f-vector of all strict distinct-vertex
triangle cap circuits. It does not claim that a general body's vector is a
mixture of these vectors.

For d=(d_1,d_2,d_3) with sum_i |d_i|<1, use cyclic indices and define

    g_i=1-d_(i+1)+d_(i+2),
    F_i(d)=sqrt(g_i^2-d_i^2).                          (1)

All roots are strictly positive: g_i-|d_i|>=1-sum |d_i|>0.

**Theorem.** The set of vectors f associated with all actual planar
triangles, interior sources, and balanced strict distinct-vertex cap
circuits is exactly the image F of the open l1 unit ball in (1). Its
closure is the continuous image of the closed l1 unit ball.

## 1. Necessity

Normalize the three positive captured-vertex margins a_i to sum to one,
and write the off-diagonal negative margins as -b_ij, all b_ij>0.
Balanced normals give the column relations sum_(i!=j)b_ij=a_j. Put

    s_i=b_i,i+1+b_i,i+2,
    d_i=b_i,i+1-b_i,i+2.

Then sum s_i=1 and |d_i|<s_i, so sum |d_i|<1. The exact column identities
give 2a_i+s_i=g_i, and the vertex-cap determinant formula gives

    f_i^2=4(a_i+b_i,i+1)(a_i+b_i,i+2)=g_i^2-d_i^2.

Thus every actual vector lies in the displayed image. These are the same
signed-row identities proved in
`candidate 919c51f1d263878e`.

## 2. An explicit actual realization of every parameter

Conversely take any d in the open l1 ball and set

    epsilon=1-sum |d_i|>0,
    s_i=|d_i|+epsilon/3,
    b_i,i+1=(s_i+d_i)/2,
    b_i,i+2=(s_i-d_i)/2,
    a_i=(g_i-s_i)/2.                                  (2)

All b_ij are positive. Also g_i-|d_i|>=epsilon, so
a_i>=epsilon/3>0. We have sum s_i=1 and sum g_i=3, hence sum a_i=1.
The cyclic formulas give exactly

    a_j=sum_(i!=j)b_ij.                               (3)

Define the 3 by 3 matrix M with diagonal a_i and off-diagonal -b_ij.
Its columns sum to zero. Each principal 2 by 2 minor is strictly positive:
for distinct i,j and remaining k, (3) gives

    a_i a_j-b_ij b_ji
      =(b_ji+b_ki)(b_ij+b_kj)-b_ij b_ji>0.

Thus M has rank exactly two. Its positive vector of principal cofactors
lies in its right kernel. This follows directly from the adjugate identity:
the left kernel is spanned by (1,1,1), so the columns of adj(M) agree and
their diagonal entries are these cofactors. Normalize this vector to a
positive vector lambda with sum lambda_i=1.

Take actual vertices in R^2 to be the first two entries of each column:

    P_j=(M_1j,M_2j),       j=1,2,3.

They are affinely independent. Indeed any affine dependence has its
coefficient vector in ker M, because the third row is minus the first two,
and also has coefficient sum zero. Since ker M is spanned by the positive
lambda whose sum is one, that vector must be zero. Moreover sum lambda_j
P_j=0, so zero is in the interior of their triangle.

For the actual balanced normals (1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1), the signed vertex
matrix is exactly M. Each row therefore strictly isolates its own vertex,
with precisely the positive and negative margins (2). The normalized cap
and coarea calculations recover F_i(d) by (1). This is an actual geometric
realization, not merely a balanced formal matrix.

## 3. Closure and scope

Formula (1) extends continuously to the closed l1 ball: g_i>=|d_i| there,
so all roots remain real and nonnegative. This compact image contains the
closure of the open image. Conversely, for any boundary parameter d, the
parameters (1-eta)d lie in the open ball and converge to d; their actual
triangle vectors converge to F(d). Hence the two closures agree exactly.

Boundary vectors may come from degenerating triangles, source incidences,
or cap sizes. No nondegenerate actual realization of every boundary point
is asserted. The theorem is a finite exact parameterization for ordinary
triangle vectors; promoting it to a domination or convex-mixture theorem
for quadrilaterals would require an additional proof.

## 4. Exact cube-slab coordinates and a stronger cubic inequality

Set

    u_i=(1+d_i-d_(i+1)+d_(i+2))/2=(g_i+d_i)/2.

Then

    f_i=2sqrt[u_i(1-u_(i+1))].                         (4)

The open l1 ball in Section 1 corresponds EXACTLY to

    0<u_i<1,       1<u_1+u_2+u_3<2.                  (5)

Indeed sum u=(3+sum d)/2, and the inverse map is
d_(i+1)=sum u-1-u_i. The eight linear inequalities defining the l1 ball
become precisely the six strict cube inequalities and the two strict sum
inequalities in (5). Thus (4)--(5) are another complete actual triangle
parameterization, not only necessary row restrictions.

Put P=u_1u_2u_3 and Q=(1-u_1)(1-u_2)(1-u_3). Expanding (4) gives the exact
nonnegative deficit

    4-sum_i f_i^2-f_1f_2f_3
       =4(sqrt(P)-sqrt(Q))^2>=0.                       (6)

To check it, sum f_i^2/4=sum u_i-sum_(i<j)u_i u_j,
and f_1f_2f_3=8sqrt(PQ); also P+Q=1-sum u_i+sum_(i<j)u_i u_j.
This proves the strictly stronger cubic triangle inequality

    f_1^2+f_2^2+f_3^2+f_1f_2f_3<=4.                  (7)

In particular it retains information that is lost when one keeps only the
three separate Lorentz rows. Each f_i lies in (0,2). With g=f_j+f_l,

    sum f_s^2+prod f_s
      =f_i^2+g^2-(2-f_i)f_j f_l
      >=f_i^2+(2+f_i)g^2/4.

Combining with (7) proves f_i+g^2/4<=2. Equality requires BOTH equality in
(7) and f_j=f_l. Thus (6) recovers the missing equality symmetry directly.

## 5. A three-by-three PSD description

For f>=0 define a symmetric matrix B(f) with zero diagonal and cyclic
off-diagonal entries

    B_i,i+1=B_i+1,i=f_i/2,

and put C(f)=I-B(f). For positive f, (7) is equivalent to C(f) being PSD.
One direction follows from its determinant

    det C(f)=1-[sum f_i^2+f_1f_2f_3]/4.

Conversely (7) implies 0<f_i<2 and hence all two-by-two principal minors
are positive. The positive first pivot and positive second leading minor,
together with the nonnegative determinant, give a PSD matrix by the usual
explicit Schur complement (or by completing two squares). At nonnegative
boundary data the same equivalence follows by continuity, or by checking
all principal minors directly. This yields a closed convex, coordinatewise
downward-closed subset

    D={f>=0:C(f) is PSD}.                              (8)

For downward closedness, if 0<=g<=f and C(f) is PSD, its nonpositive
off-diagonals give, for every real x,

    x^T C(g)x >= |x|^T C(g)|x|
                 >=|x|^T C(f)|x|>=0.

## 6. Every positive PSD vector is dominated by an actual triangle vector

The converse geometric statement for the downward closure is exact:

**Triangle domination theorem.** For every positive f in D there is an
actual strict distinct-vertex triangle vector f' with f'>=f coordinatewise.
It may be chosen on the same ray, f'=f/rho for some 0<rho<=1.

Choose a unit vector maximizing the Rayleigh quotient of B(f). Compactness
of the sphere gives a maximizer, and replacing its coordinates by absolute
values cannot decrease the quadratic form because B(f) is nonnegative.
Thus its largest eigenvalue rho has a nonnegative eigenvector w. Since
the three off-diagonal edge weights are positive, w is strictly positive:
a zero coordinate in B(f)w=rho w forces every neighbor to vanish. The
eigenvalue is positive, for example by evaluating the form on (1,1,1).
The condition I-B(f) PSD implies rho<=1.

Set f'=f/rho and c_i=f'_i/2, so B(f')w=w. Define

    u_i=c_i w_(i+1)/w_i.

At node i, the eigenvector equation has two positive summands, so
0<u_i<1. At node i+1, it gives

    1-u_(i+1)=c_i w_i/w_(i+1).

Consequently u_i(1-u_(i+1))=c_i^2, which is exactly (4) for f'. Moreover

    prod u_i=prod c_i=prod(1-u_i).

This equality implies 1<sum u_i<2. To see the lower inequality, expand
the product equality as sum u_i=1+sum_(i<j)u_i u_j-2prod u_i; each pair
product exceeds prod u_i, so the right side exceeds one. Apply the same
argument to the three complements to get the upper inequality.

Thus u satisfies the exact domain (5). Sections 1--2 construct an ACTUAL
strict triangle realizing f'. Since rho<=1, it dominates f as claimed.

It follows that D is precisely the closed coordinatewise downward hull,
and hence also the closed downward convex hull, of actual strict triangle
vectors. The positive part already has an attained single-triangle
dominator; no convex combination is needed there. To include zero
coordinates, approximate any f in D by positive interior vectors, for
example (1-epsilon)f+epsilon(1,1,1)/2. Their matrices are convex
combinations of C(f) and the positive-definite C((1,1,1)/2), hence are
positive definite for epsilon>0. Apply the positive case and pass to a
subsequence in the compact closed triangle image from Section 3. The
limiting triangle-limit vector dominates f.

The statement is about the geometry of the EXACT triangle f-image. Showing
that arbitrary quadrilateral or convex-body data belong to D remains a
separate stronger inequality, not a consequence of the parameterization
or of the known three individual row inequalities. No such promotion is
asserted here.
